See: 32 N.J.R. 2565(a), 32 N.J.R. 3844(a). Substituted "CBOSS" for "CWA" throughout. Amended by R.2012 d.025, effective February 6, 2012. See: 43 N.J.R. 804(a), 44 N.J.R. 230(a). Substituted "CWAs" for "CBOSSs" and "CWA" for "CBOSS" throughout; in (a), substituted "that" for "which"; in (c)4, inserted "and" at the end; in (c)5, substituted a period for a semicolon at the end; recodified former (c)6 as (d) and former (d) as (e); and in (e)2, substituted "his or her" for "his/her" and inserted "and" at the end. Annotations Notes Chapter Notes Case Notes Final agency decision properly affirmed the imposition of a transfer penalty upon a claimant's application for Medicaid benefits to pay for the cost of her nursing home care because a life care contract between herself and her daughter made as a lump sum advance payment to the daughter was not a transfer for fair market value. E.S. v. Division of Med. Assistance & Health Servs., 412 N.J. Super. 340, 990 A.2d 701, 2010 N.J. Super. LEXIS 47 (2010). Medicaid application made on behalf of a divorced wife was properly denied for failure to provide verification of information relative to her assets and financial transactions. Specifically, the applicant failed to submit documentation confirming her claims relative to several large disbursements including $ 5000 that allegedly was spent to repair her kitchen, $ 1000 that allegedly was spent to repair her bathroom, and various amounts that were claimed to have been lost in a scam. Moreover, because the applicant claimed to have sent funds to her ex- husband's attorney in connection with the couple's divorce but did not substantiate that expense, the applicant did not carry her burden to rebut the presumption that the transfer was made for establish Medicaid eligibility. F.R. v. Monmouth Cty. Div. of Soc. Serv., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 07300-23, 2024 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 112, Initial Decision (January 16, 2024). Authorized representative of an applicant for Medicaid benefits failed to show that either the applicant's death, which occurred while the application was pending, or the death of her caseworker was the cause of the representative's failure to obtain and submit documentation requested in connection with the application. That was because much of the requested documentation that was still outstanding at the time of the denial of the application, from which this appeal was taken, was either requested while the applicant was still alive or was within the control of either the representative or the applicant's granddaughter. Thus, no exceptional circumstances existed justifying additional time to provide the requested documentation. E.W. v. DMAHS et al., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 03229-2021, 2021 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 421, Final Agency Determination (October 26, 2021). Where the applicant's Designated Authorized Representative (DAR) repeatedly failed to provide the requested documentation to determine eligibility, the Medicaid application was appropriately denied. The DAR and the applicant's spouse had 182 days from the first verification letter to the deadline set forth in the last verification letter to request, receive, and submit the information. The DAR's failure to timely request the documentation regarding

body: Page 3 of 14 § 10:71-2.2 Responsibilities in the application process the spouse's life insurance policy did not create a necessity for an extension of time. M.D. v. Div. of Med. Assistance and Health Servs., et al., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 11056-2020, 2021 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 234, Final Agency Determination (June 29, 2021). Determination of a county welfare agency that an applicant for Medicaid was not entitled to benefits based on its finding that the applicant had not timely provided information needed to determine his eligibility was reversed and remanded for additional proceedings on the ground that where, as here, several Medicaid applications had been filed, the review of the applicant's financial history had to be based on the five year period that was prior to the first of such applications. That being so, the "look-back" period for this applicant was the five-year period prior to the first application, which was filed in 2018, rather than the most recent application, filed in October 2019. J.G. v. Morris Cnty. Dep't of Family Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 04827-20, 2021 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 52, Order Reversing and Remanding Denial of Benefits (February 23, 2021). DMAHS rejected the claim of a Medicaid recipient who had been granted a January 1 eligibility date that the agency had lacked the authority to impose a transfer penalty based on the agency's post-eligibility discovery that the recipient had transferred the proceeds of sale of her residence to her daughter within the 60-month look-back period. The transfer penalty was imposed subsequent to the issuance of the notice of eligibility because the recipient had failed to disclose the transfer and there was no merit to the recipient's position that the agency should be prevented from imposing the transfer penalty on these facts. MM v. Middlesex Cnty. Bd. of Soc. Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 05078-19, 2020 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 54, Final Agency Determination (January 27, 2020). Application for Medicaid was properly denied on findings that the applicant failed to comply with a request for documentation prior to the deadline set by the county board of social services inasmuch as she did not provide the board with her current monthly pension statement for a stated year, investment account statements or a plan for the liquidation of certain insurance policies. C.C. v. Burlington Cnty. Bd. of Soc. Servs., OAL DKT. NO.HMA 14778-19, 2019 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 1052, Initial Decision (December 20, 2019). Applicant for Medicaid only benefits was entitled to a retroactive date of eligibility. The applicant diligently undertook to provide information requested about an annuity. If the board of social services had not made an error in reassigning her file, the documents would have been provided within the period set by law. Delays resulting from administrative error at the board were not properly permitted to affect the applicant's retroactive eligibility date. M.A. v. Monmouth Cnty. Bd. of Soc. Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 07879-19, 2019 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 558, Final Agency Determination (August 27, 2019). Medicaid application was properly denied over the applicant's claim that the deadline should have been extended to allow him to provide requested items because the agency in fact had extended the deadline for receipt of the requested items from July 19 to December 13, and the applicant still failed to provide the needed documentation. M.S. v. Gloucester Cnty., Bd. of Soc. Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 02481-18, 2018 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 794, Final Agency Determination (June 25, 2018). Lawyers who were conservators for an elderly man who was applying for Medicaid nursing home disabled benefits were acting in good faith to transmit all required documentation to a county social services board and their conduct also reflected cooperation and proactive efforts to comply with the board's requests. Those efforts constituted "exceptional circumstances" within the meaning of Medicaid Communication 10-09 and justified an order reversing the benefit denial and requiring a review of the application. H.P. v. Ocean Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 01118-18, 2018 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 271, Initial Decision (May 11, 2018). Though no exceptions were filed, the DMAHS director modified the ALJ's determination that a board of social services had failed to assist the applicant in the Medicaid application process. While the board could have specifically requested the second page of the lawsuit, the applicant could have also inquired what was missing upon receiving the board's second request for a complete copy. This was the applicant's fourth application and his representative was familiar with the process and the requirement to provide information. A.A. v. DMAHS, et al., OAL Docket No. HMA 13178-17, 2018 N.J. AGEN. LEXIS 129, Final Agency Determination (January 29, 2018).

body: Page 4 of 14 § 10:71-2.2 Responsibilities in the application process DMAHS Director reversed an ALJ's Initial Decision in favor of a Medicaid applicant and reinstated an agency ruling denying benefits on the ground that the applicant failed to provide the needed information prior to the date on which benefits were denied and that the determination notice issued by the agency sufficiently set out the action that the agency was taking, the rationale therefor and the statutes that supported the proposed action. D.C. v. DMAHS, OAL DKT. NO. HMA 06870-17, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 1310, Final Agency Determination (December 7, 2017). Once a Medicaid recipient was declared incompetent by reason of dementia, he in fact did not have "access" to the cash value of his life insurance policies for the purpose of resource counting and that value could not be used as a basis to terminate his benefits based on the existence of excess resources. Nor was a delay in the verification of financial information good grounds to terminate the recipient's benefits. Both of these circumstances were byproducts of a five-month delay between the filing of a verified complaint for guardianship in the Superior Court and the issuance, by that court, of an order granting the same and the additional delay occasioned by the guardian's need to obtain Letters of Guardianship and a related bond. R.P. v. Gloucester Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 05302-17, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 734, Initial Decision (September 28, 2017). Determination of county social services board denying a Medicaid application made on behalf of a disabled woman who died during the pendency of the proceedings was rejected by an ALJ on findings that the board failed to comply with the 90-day statutory time frame for decision, failed to advise the applicant's representative as to why the application was not being determined on a timely basis, allowed 570 days to elapse between the date of application and the date of denial, and otherwise failed to comply with its obligations vis-a-vis the application. D.C. v. Burlington Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 6870-17, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 727, Initial Decision (September 18, 2017). Though no exceptions were filed, the DMAHS director reversed the Initial Decision of an ALJ finding that the daughter of a Medicaid applicant who had since died had provided sufficient verification for the applicant to be considered for Medicaid benefits and that the agency should accept such documentation with an original application date and instead concluded that the credible evidence established that the daughter had failed to provide the needed information prior to the date of denial and that the agency properly concluded that it was unable to determine the applicant's income or whether her QIT was fully funded. S.A. v. Union Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 3094-17, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 1046, Final Agency Determination (September 8, 2017). ALJ rejected an agency determination denying Medicaid benefits to an applicant, which denial was based on the agency's finding that the applicant had failed to provide required verifications. The evidence tended to show that the applicant's representative in fact provided most of the requested documents prior to the deadline and timely requested clarification of some of the requested items, which clarification was not timely provided. Nor was the agency's claim that the documents should have been included in tabbed volumes sufficient to justify the agency's denial. S.I.K. v. Passaic Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 03882-17, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 703, Initial Decision (September 8, 2017). There was nothing in state or federal law governing the application for and grant or denial of Medicaid benefits that excused an applicant from her obligation to obtain documents needed to verify her eligibility or required the county social services board to obtain documents not available through the Asset Verification System (AVS) system. J.F. v. DMAHS et al., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 03786-17, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 1047, Final Agency Determination (August 29, 2017). Social services board acted properly in denying an application by a Medicaid applicant for Qualified Income Trust (QIT) Nursing Home Medicaid benefits based on the applicant's failure to assist the board due to her failure to provide requested documentation. Though a copy of the "Family Trust" was submitted, the schedules that were related to the Trust and were submitted to the board were blank. That meant that the applicant had failed to submit information that adequately documented the inventory of the trust. It was not the duty of the board to secure such information independently. L.A. v. Monmouth Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 6627-17, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 651, Initial Decision (August 23, 2017).

body: Page 5 of 14 § 10:71-2.2 Responsibilities in the application process Applicant was properly denied Skilled Nursing Home Medicaid benefits on the ground that the applicant had failed to provide information relating to a bank account. Information concerning that account was requested in three of four letters from the agency, which also indicated that any further extensions of time had to be approved by a unit supervisor. Because the applicant neither provided the requested information nor requested another extension, denial of the application was proper. H.H. v. Camden Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 08680-17, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 629, Initial Decision (August 21, 2017). Interpretation of regulations that was urged by an applicant for Nursing Home Medicaid Claimant's as imposing the burden to establish eligibility therefor upon a country social services board was contrary to the language and import of N.J.A.C. 10:71-2.2 and N.J.A.C. 10:71-3.1(b), both of which require the applicant to substantiate claims of eligibility with corroborative evidence from pertinent sources. L.K. v. Camden Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 17513-16, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 551, Initial Decision (July 11, 2017). Agency should not have denied an application for Medicaid Only filed by a daughter on behalf of her elderly mother because the daughter showed that she provided most of the requested documents in a timely manner, that certain pension information requested by the agency was not available to her, and that her status as POA for her mother had terminated upon the latter's death. S.A. v. Union Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 03094-17, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 500, Initial Decision (July 6, 2017). Social service agency failed to carry out its assigned responsibilities when it failed to advise the representatives of a Medicaid applicant that there were documents that had been requested by the agency but had not been supplied. That is, the agency had a responsibility to sufficiently communicate with the applicant to explain why previous submissions were insufficient. J.D. v. Essex Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 03198-17, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 398, Initial Decision (June 20, 2017). Applicant for institutional-level Medicaid did not carry her burden to show that a county welfare agency failed to provide effective assistance in connection with requests for documentation from applicant. Applicant's representative did not provide basic banking information to the agency. In the absence of such, there was nothing that the agency could do in the way of verifying accuracy or otherwise advancing the application, so denial thereof was not improper. P.R. v. Union Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 09905-16, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 401, Initial Decision (June 16, 2017).Director approved of and adopted ALJ's report and recommendation finding that the failure and/or refusal of a husband of an incapacitated wife to disclose his resources in connection with a redetermination of the wife's Medicaid eligibility did not provide grounds to either extend the time for compliance or grant a "spousal waiver." K.Z. v. DMAHS, OAL DKT. NO. HMA 16945-16, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 1143, Final Agency Determination (May 23, 2017). Agency's denial of an application for Medicaid nursing home benefits on the ground that agency requests for information were unfulfilled was reversed because, unbeknown to the agency, applicant's wife, who was responding to the agency's information requests, had been hospitalized as a result of a fall and spent several weeks in a rehabilitation facility. Given those unforeseen circumstances, the applicant's wife should have been allowed additional time to respond to the agency's follow-up requests. R.B. v. Burlington Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NOS. HMA 14375-16, HMA 04295-16 (Consolidated), 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 313, Initial Decision (May 15, 2017). ALJ's determination that an applicant's first Medicaid application was properly denied was approved by the Director, but the ALJ's finding reversing the county social services board's ruling that a second application should not be denied was rejected by the Director. The fact that the applicant's wife, who was responding to the agency's information requests, had been hospitalized due to a fall and had spent several weeks in a rehabilitation facility was an insufficient basis for relief because the applicant at all times was represented by counsel. That meant that "exceptional circumstances" justifying an extension of the deadline for submission of verifications were not shown. R.B. v. DMAHS, OAL DKT. NO. HMA 04295-16, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 1169, Final Agency Determination (May 13, 2017).

body: Page 6 of 14 § 10:71-2.2 Responsibilities in the application process Claims by a Medicaid applicant that the county agency had a duty to obtain certain banking statements relating to her assets was unsupported by law because the regulations were clear that such materials were required to be obtained by the applicant or her agents. This was especially true because the applicant did not state, in any of her applications, that she needed assistance in completing the applications. V.S. v. Bergen Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 08041-16, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 249, Initial Decision (April 26, 2017). Applicant for Medicaid won limited relief on claims that her eligibility date was properly based on an application that she made on May 8, 2015 as opposed to on a second application dated August 23, 2016. The social services board had violated various regulations in connection with the earlier application, which it apparently had misplaced, so it was properly ordered to dispose of the May 8 application within 45 days of the ruling. S.D. v. Essex Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 02582-17, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 181, Initial Decision (March 29, 2017). Community spouse (applicant) who represented to a county temporary support office that the applicant's son was paying the applicant's housing expenses was not entitled to any relief from his payment obligations. Though the applicant originally advised the agency that his son was paying his expenses, presumably as a gift, after consulting a different elder law attorney, the applicant asserted that the son was "lending" the funds to the applicant. On these facts, which included the applicant's submission of a promissory note that appeared to have been backdated, the applicant was not entitled to relief on his claim that the funds were a loan or that the agency should have counseled the applicant from the outset that characterizing the son's funds as a "loan" would be financially advantageous. E.B. v. Morris Cnty. Office of Temporary Assistance, OAL DKT. NO. HMA 14388-16, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 94, Initial Decision (February 10, 2017). Agency did not err in denying a Medicaid application because applicant neither supplied the requested information about resources nor requested that the agency assist her in obtaining missing documentation. E.F. v. Essex Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 09216-16, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 72, Initial Decision (February 3, 2017). Agency's denial of a Medicaid application based on the applicant's failure to provide requested information was reversed because the applicant had made many attempts to obtain them. The agency, though required to assist the applicant, in fact had made no effort to assist by utilizing either AVS or PARIS and thus could not properly deny the application based on missing information. Moreover, the resulting delay was beyond the applicant's control and could not be used as a basis for denial. C.F.J. v. Hudson Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 06589-16 (Remand of HMA 04859-14), 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 50, Initial Decision (January 31, 2017). Original denial of Medicaid application was proper despite the fact that the applicant belatedly provided requested documentation because the applicant's failure to timely provide such verifications that led to the denial. It was not the agency's duty to organize and summarize raw data in the form of deposit slips or checking-account registers to determine dates of deposits and expenses paid by the applicant and/or family members in order to determine eligibility. V.W. v. DMAHS, OAL DKT. NO. HMA 12941-16, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 52, Initial Decision (January 27, 2017). Medicaid applicant won retroactive eligibility date because the social services agency responsible for acting on his application failed to timely move the case through the approval process, failed to give the applicant required notifications, failed to assist the applicant and failed to independently verify the value of resources. The overall failure on the part of the agency justified a retroactive date. W.M. v. Union Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 11651-16, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 27, Initial Decision (January 18, 2017). A Medicaid applicant's failure to provide verification relating to funds referenced on bank statements, funds borrowed against life insurance and other, similar items afforded adequate grounds for the decision of a social services board to deny that application. body: Page 7 of 14 § 10:71-2.2 Responsibilities in the application process demonstrate they either asked for or that there were exceptional circumstances warranting additional time to provide the requested verifications. J.B. v. DMAHS, OAL DKT. NO. HMA 9587-2016, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 1374, Final Administrative Determination (December 15, 2016). Failure on the part of the representative for a nursing home resident to submit required documentation despite the issuance of numerous extensions of the deadline afforded grounds for a denial of Medicaid eligibility. A.D. v. Cape May Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 10418-16, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 1236, Initial Decision (December 8, 2016). County social services board erred in denying an application for Medicaid for a claimed failure to provide required verifications because some of the items that the board claimed had not been provided in response to its original notification in fact had not been requested and the board failed to respond to a request by the applicant for a reasonable extension of the deadline to allow other materials to be submitted. S.I.K. v. Passaic Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 11596-16, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 1013, Initial Decision (December 5, 2016). County social services board did not err in denying an application for Medicaid for the applicant's failure to provide required verifications because it had granted two extensions to the applicant to allow her to provide missing information and the applicant's ongoing failure to provide needed information afforded grounds for denial of the application. S.C. v. Camden Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 11683-16, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 1014, Initial Decision (November 30, 2016). Though the ALJ recognized that employee of a county social services board had mishandled the Medicaid application made by a husband on behalf of his institutionalized wife, the ALJ lacked the power to provide an "equitable" remedy because the wife was not Medicaid-eligible until the spend-down was completed. However, the ALJ encouraged the Commissioner to exercise any discretion possessed by the Commissioner's office in order to address the seemingly unfair result. A.S. v. DMAHS and Monmouth Cnty. Div. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 13504-16, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 1015, Initial Decision (November 4, 2016). Applicant's challenge to an order denying Medicaid eligibility on findings that there was no verification of certain deductions from insurance policies failed because the social services board made clear requests for such information and the nursing home that was acting for the applicant failed to provide the requested information. J.B. v. Camden Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 09587-16, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 955, Initial Decision (November 3, 2016). Agency should not have denied a Medicaid application on a finding that required financial verifications were not provided but should have granted additional time to the applicant to obtain the requested documents because the applicant's representative made ongoing concerted efforts to obtain the requested documents and had promptly advised the agency of the difficulties that were being encountered by the representative in trying to obtain documents from a financial institution that had been acquired by another institution. W.S. v. DMAHS et al., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 11145-16, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 866, Initial Decision (October 21, 2016). Though the agency failed to promptly process an application for Medicaid Only nursing home benefits and failed to advise the applicant of the reason for delay, the failure of the agency to advise the applicant of what needed to occur for eligibility to be determined was not grounds for an eligibility date that was earlier than that granted by the agency because the applicant was not resource-eligible earlier than the date awarded. W.H. v. Monmouth Cnty. Div. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 10917-16, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 862, Initial Decision (October 19, 2016). Application for Medicaid was properly denied because the applicant, despite receiving three deadline extensions, failed to provide documentation repeatedly requested by a county social services board. M.M. v. Camden Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 03870-16, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 820, Initial Decision (October 3, 2016). Medicaid recipient's benefits were properly terminated on findings that he did not demonstrate, as required, that he in fact was not the owner of an LLC in whose name a utility bill was received because the recipient had the

body: Page 8 of 14 § 10:71-2.2 Responsibilities in the application process responsibility to complete any forms required as part of the application process but had failed to do so. A.F. v. Middlesex Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 09620-16, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 824, Initial Decision (October 3, 2016). Social services board acted properly in requesting income verification for a deceased nursing home resident for the two month period between August 1, 2015, the date of Medicaid eligibility requested by counsel, and the date of application, which was October 22, 2015, because the governing regulations made it clear that the month of application determined resource eligibility even if one was seeking eligibility from a date two months prior to the application. P.S. v. Camden Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 05515-16, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 755, Initial Decision (September 9, 2016). County social services board adequately fulfilled its obligation to assist a nursing home employee who was making a Medicaid application on behalf of an aged resident by giving them over a year to obtain specified financial information. The resident had no family and limited ability to assist. Where, as here, the employee failed to provide income verifications despite best efforts and the granting of extensions, the board was justified in denying eligibility. R.S. v. Camden Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 6126-16, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 696, Initial Decision (August 2, 2016). Social services board acted lawfully when it denied an application for Nursing Home/Institutional Medicaid on the ground that additional verification documentation was needed to establish eligibility and that partial documentation was not provided prior to the deadline. The applicant's son delivered the documentation to the wrong county agency because he did not want to stand in line at the Board's office, but the existence of a long line was not an exceptional circumstance excusing the son's failure to comply with the deadline. U.R. v. Camden Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 04290-16, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 709, Initial Decision (July 29, 2016). Application for Medicaid benefits by nursing home resident should not have been denied on the ground, as claimed by the agency, that the resident had not cooperated with the agency's requests for additional information. The denial was issued only four days after the resident's representative advised the agency that requested information was forthcoming and the requested materials were provided on the day after the denial was issued. The agency's denial thus was unreasonable. A.H. v. Essex Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 09245-16, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 647, Initial Decision (July 26, 2016). Medicaid applicant who was never notified of the need to provide documentation could not be denied benefits on the ground that he did not provide that documentation. L.B. v. DMAHS and Essex Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 05732-16, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 645, Initial Decision (July 26, 2016). Even though the agency did not make much of a showing that it had met its responsibility to assist the son of an applicant in completing an application for Global Options Medicaid benefits, the facts did show that the agency had given the applicant's son about 18 months to obtain five years of financial records. That being the case, the agency's action denying the application was properly sustained. D.M. v. Camden Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs. et al, OAL DKT. NO. HMA 04971-16, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 404, Initial Decision (May 26, 2016). Agency director rejected ALJ's finding that a county social services board had acted properly in determining that an applicant was ineligible for Medicaid. The agency failed to show any reason for the delay in processing the application, did not show that the applicant failed to provide necessary verifications, and failed to show that the applicant had excess resources. N.V. v. DMAHS and Gloucester Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 01201-16, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 642, Final Administrative Determination (May 5, 2016). Son's failure to obtain and provide, to a county board of social services, true copies of agreements and related documents concerning a trust of which his father, an elderly man who was disabled due to Alzheimers, dementia and Parkinson's disease, was the sole trustee afforded grounds for a denial of Medicaid benefits. This was notwithstanding the fact that the son had demonstrated that the documents were not provided because the son simply could not obtain them from the bank where the trust was established. body: Page 9 of 14 § 10:71-2.2 Responsibilities in the application process Assistance & Health Services and Camden Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 20582-15, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 156, Initial Decision (March 28, 2016). Because a county board of social services was entitled to establish a cut-off date for submission, by an applicant, of information requested by the board and needed to determine whether the applicant was eligible for Medicaid, the determination that the applicant had failed to submit needed materials was properly affirmed. While a county board had the option to afford additional time to an applicant, it nonetheless was entitled to determine when sufficient time was allowed and to make a decision based on the information in its possession on the deadline. N.V. v. DMAHS and Gloucester Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs.,OAL DKT. NO. HMA 01201-16, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 140, Initial Decision (March 17, 2016). County board of social services did not comply with required deadlines in governing regulations when it considered whether a petitioner's eligibility for "Medicaid Only" Institutional Medicaid, with the result that the eligibility date of July 1, 2015 that was granted by the board was incorrect and the petitioner was entitled to an eligibility date of May 1, 2015. Among other failures, the board did not comply with its duty to write to the petitioner and explain the reasons for delay and failed to inform the petitioner of the need for a Qualified Income Trust (QIT) in a timely manner. Because the manner in which the board processed the application was improper, an earlier eligibility date was appropriately granted. J.E., Petitioner, v. Passaic Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 15778-15, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 120, Initial Decision (March 10, 2016). County social services board was justified in denying an application for Medicaid on the ground that the applicant had failed to provide verification of resources per governing regulations. The board gave the applicant more than two months to provide closing statements from certain investment accounts. On these facts, the board took reasonable steps and gave adequate time for the applicant to submit the required verification. M.B. v. Ocean Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 14682-15, 2015 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 758, Initial Decision (December 22, 2015). Failure on the part of an applicant seeking Medicaid benefits for the Adult Medicaid Nursing Home program to submit required documentation and to otherwise cooperate with the agency in determining eligibility justified the agency in denying the application, which denial was sustained following a fair hearing. Though the facility in which the applicant resided claimed to have submitted the requested documents via facsimile, the facility offered no substantiation such as a fax transmittal confirmation. Because the requested documents were not submitted until the day of the hearing, which was well after they were required to be submitted, the agency's denial of the application was properly approved. A.B. v. Essex Cty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 03840-15, 2015 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 234, Initial Decision (May 4, 2015). Medicaid eligibility of a recipient was properly terminated on a finding that an absent parent of the recipient's younger minor child in fact lived with the recipient notwithstanding the recipient's denial that the absent parent in fact resided with her and two children. The recipient's testimony relative to where the absent parent was living was unworthy of belief in the face of other evidence that established that the recipient in fact currently was in a romantic relationship with the absent parent and that the latter's last known address was that at which the recipient currently resided. Nor had the recipient provided the agency with adequate information establishing that the absent parent in fact resided elsewhere. K.B. v. Gloucester Cty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 02927-15, 2015 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 233, Initial Decision (April 30, 2015). An Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) concluded that an applicant was eligible for Medicaid and that denial of his application was improper. The grounds for the denial was that the agency was not satisfied with the applicant's explanation that numerous $ 9000 deposits made into his checking account reflected cash that he had squirreled away over many years. The agency believed that the funds had been derived from other assets that had not been adequately disclosed. However, the applicant's testimony relative to the source of the funds was fully corroborated by the former executive director of an assisted living complex in which the applicant had resided, who testified that she had first-hand knowledge that the applicant had nearly $ 80,000 in cash, funds that he had retained in cash because he did not trust banks. Because the corroboration of the source of funds that was required by the

body: Page 10 of 14 § 10:71-2.2 Responsibilities in the application process regulations had been provided, the ALJ concluded that the applicant should not have been denied Medicaid eligibility. W.F. v. Monmouth Cty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 16564-14, 2015 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 264, Initial Decision (April 17, 2015). Determinations of the Division of Medical Assistance and Health Services (DMAHS) twice denying Medicaid benefits on behalf of an applicant who died during the pendency of the application denying the application on the ground that the applicant's wife (and, later, widow) had not produced two insurance policies was rejected by an administrative law judge (ALJ). Though the policies were ultimately produced after having been located by an attorney retained by the widow to assist her in handling her deceased spouse's estate, the widow's age, infirmities and mental and emotional status during the application period rendered her incapable of assisting DMAHS and providing the necessary documents. Those conditions constituted "exceptional circumstances" within the meaning of relevant regulations that warranted an extension of time to provide the documents. The ALJ noted in so finding that the purpose of the regulatory scheme was to facilitate disposition of a Medicaid application on the merits. So long as there was good reason for a failure to provide all documentation, the better practice would be to extend the deadline, obtain all relevant information, and make a determination of the merits. J.F. v. DMAHS and Cumberland Cty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 9678-14 and HMA 17109-14 (CONSOLIDATED), 2015 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 189, Initial Decision (March 6, 2015). Determination by a county board of social services (BSS) denying an application for Medicaid eligibility filed by a nursing home on behalf of a resident therein was not supported by the record because the evidence showed that the resident's condition was such that she could not assist the home in collecting the bank statements that the BSS had requested and the home had made substantial efforts to gather and provide the information requested. Though agreeing that all of the documentation had not been provided, the administrative law judge (ALJ) found that given the resident's inability to assist in assembling the materials and the efforts made to date by the home, denial of eligibility at this time was not appropriate and the home should be afforded additional time within which to try and gather the remaining materials. S.H. v. Essex Cty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 16991-14, 2015 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 188, Initial Decision (March 6, 2015). Determination by a county Board of Social Services (CBSS) denying Medicaid benefits to an applicant on the ground that the applicant had failed to provide required verification and had failed to assist the CBSS in securing relevant documentation was rejected by an administrative law judge. The applicant was a 71 year old who suffered from both psychiatric and physical conditions, and his application had been filed by his estranged wife, from whom he had been separated for 10 years. The testimonial and documentary evidence in the record supported the wife's position that she had responded to the best of her ability to the requests made by the caseworker and was attempting to cooperate with the agency to the extent that she could. A fair reading of the governing regulations showed that there were circumstances where the processing of an application would be delayed beyond the time that was normally essential and that the circumstances of this case were such that the agency should have afforded more time to the wife to address documentation requests made by the caseworker. On that basis, the application was properly reinstated. R.C. v. Camden Cty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 13064-2014, 2015 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 205, Initial Decision (February 12, 2015). Determination that a former resident of a nursing home located in Burlington County was not eligible for Medicaid on account of his failure to provide a verification of his wife's resources or a letter indicating that she had no assets was properly sustained. The original notice to the nursing home, which had filed the application on behalf of the resident while the resident was still residing in its facility, advised that such documents had to be provided no later than October 26, 2013. When the nursing home contacted the Burlington County Board of Social Services (BCBSS) in August of 2014, it advised BCBSS that the resident had left the facility in February 2014 and had been approved for Medicaid in a different county. Given the record as of that date, denial of Medicaid eligibility for failure to provide the requested verification was proper. M.P. v. Burlington Cty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 12429-14, 2015 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 114, Initial Decision (February 11, 2015). Although no Medicaid statute or regulation specifically refers to a "spousal waiver," New Jersey's Medicaid program informally recognizes the existence of such a waiver, and in appropriate cases an applicant is properly

body: Page 11 of 14 § 10:71-2.2 Responsibilities in the application process exempted from the requirement of a spousal resource assessment. Such a waiver was properly found here, where the applicant and her spouse had been formally separated since 2004. Other facts that were relevant to the determination included that while the spouse had repeatedly promised to provide such records, he had failed to do so and in fact had asserted that he was not subject to court orders requiring him to submit financial records in connection with the applicant's divorce petition; that the husband had been unfailingly recalcitrant and decidedly deceptive in his dealings with the applicant and the court; and that the applicant should not be penalized on account of the husband's conduct. That meant that the applicant was entitled to have her application for benefits evaluated without regard to the husband's financial condition. N.O. v. Morris Cty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 10246-14, 2015 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 110, Initial Decision (February 11, 2015). Determination by a county Board of Social Services (CBSS) denying Medicaid benefits to an applicant on the ground that the applicant had failed to provide required information was rejected by an Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) on findings that the agency had ignored applicable regulations. Because the applicant had Alzheimer's and was confined to a nursing home, she was unable to assist her daughters, who filed the application on her behalf. To the extent that the application was denied on the ground that the daughters had not cooperated, the record did not support that position because that provision concerns cases where an applicant or her representative did not cooperate. Here, the daughters clearly were cooperating to the best of their ability. Moreover, there could be a basis for concluding that the failure to obtain verification of a single item in the amount of $ 45.88 was the fault of the agency, which might have had more success in dealing with the insurance company that had issued it. Finally, though there was authority for the agency's proposition that the normal deadline for compliance had passed, the regulation also recognized that there were circumstances where the processing of an application would be delayed beyond the time that was normally utilized and the agency should have allowed additional time. On that basis, the matter was properly remanded to the agency for a disposition on the merits. M.D. v. DMAHS and Atlantic Cty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 14997-14, 2015 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 210, Initial Decision (February 10, 2015). Nursing home resident's application for Medicaid benefits was not properly denied on the basis claimed by the agency, which was that the resident had not provided sufficient verification of factors related to eligibility, including sources of income and resources. Though the agency claimed that there were three items that had not been provided and that the denial was based on that omission, the resident in fact demonstrated that all documents with the exception of one account verification had been provided to the agency and that telephone calls to the agency to confirm that the documents as provided were sufficient were not returned. On these facts, the agency's demand, on May 23, 2014, for additional documentation after it had had no contact with the resident for five months and its cognate refusal to respond to the resident's request for additional time to provide that last item was arbitrary and unreasonable. R.D. v. Camden Cty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 9056-14, 2015 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 127, Initial Decision (January 29, 2015). Department of Medical Assistance and Health Services and the Atlantic County Board of Social Services appropriately denied an application for Medicaid benefits for failure to provide required documentation pursuant to N.J.A.C. 10:71-2.2(e). Contrary to the applicant's assertion, the denial determination provided adequate notice regarding the required documentation. To require that the Medicaid denial determination provide the specific documents the agency alleged were not provided would be to unnecessarily broaden the definition of adequate notice found in the case law or federal regulations. This was particularly true in this matter where it was clear that the applicant's attorney acknowledged the request for specific information only one week before the Medicaid denial determination. R.P. v. Div. of Med. Assistance and Health Serv. and Atlantic County Bd. of Social Serv., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 07818-14, 2014 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 778, Initial Decision (November 25, 2014). When an applicant failed to provide timely and sufficient verification to be considered for Medicaid eligibility as required by N.J.A.C. 10:71-2.2(e)2, the county welfare office properly denied the application. Although the applicant argued that his estranged spouse was uncooperative and hindered his ability to provide the requested documents and spend down verification, he did not request any additional extensions or do anything about the uncooperative spouse until several months after the application was filed. There was no evidence that the applicant advised the board of these exceptional circumstances or that he requested additional extensions as a result of the

body: Page 12 of 14 § 10:71-2.2 Responsibilities in the application process uncooperative spouse pursuant to N.J.A.C. 10:71-2.3(c). Camden County Bd. of Social Serv., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 6383-14, 2014 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 759, Initial Decision (November 20, 2014). Where the representatives of a Medicaid applicant failed to request additional time to obtain and provide additional materials requested by a board of social services, the agency cannot be said to have erred in not allowing additional time because it was not requested. Nor was there any showing of "exceptional circumstances" that would justify a grant of additional time. J.B. v. DMAHS and Cape May Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 9983-14, 2014 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 1311, Final Administrative Determination (November 14, 2014). Denial by the Sussex County Board of Social Services (Agency) of an application for Medicaid benefits by the long-term care facility from which the applicant received care was unreasonable because the facility did not fail to provide the Agency with verification information under N.J.A.C. 10:71-2.2(e). The facility submitted the requested documentation concerning the disability retirement, health benefits, or early reduced benefits from the Motion Picture Industry that were applied for, and the problem presented was that the denial letter from Motion Picture Industry was not clear. This confusion very easily could have been clarified if the Agency had persisted in its attempts to speak to a representative of the Motion Picture Industry. H.M. v. Sussex County Bd. of Social Serv., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 04381-14, 2014 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 739, Initial Decision (November 14, 2014). Failure by a Medicaid applicant to notify a county board of social services that she had changed her address was the reason that the agency could not locate the applicant and thus properly terminated her benefits. That being so, the board's action in terminating the benefits was proper. F.H. v. DMAHS et al., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 09702-14, 2014 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 1329, Final Administrative Determination (November 6, 2014). Hudson County Board of Social Services properly terminated a Medicaid recipient pursuant to N.J.A.C. 10:71- 2.2(d). Her failure to provide the agency with an address where she could be contacted and her failure to provide the post office with a forwarding address resulted in her not being able to be located. F.H. v. Hudson County Bd. of Social Serv., OAL DKT. NO. HMA09702-14, 2014 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 534, Initial Decision (November 2, 2014). When an applicant did not provide sufficient verification documentation for the Union County Board of Social Services to consider her application as required by N.J.A.C. 10:71-2.2(e)1 and N.J.A.C. 10:71-3.1(b), she could not be considered eligible for Medicaid benefits. The Board notified the applicant by letter on at least two occasions of the verification documentation that was needed to establish her eligibility, but she failed to prove the entire PA-5 report. N.R. v. Union Cnty. Bd. of Social Serv., OAL DKT. No. HMA 07734-14, 2014 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 449, Initial Decision (July 30, 2014). When an applicant failed to provide the Camden County Board of Social Services with verification documentation that was appropriately requested, the Board properly denied his application for Medicaid Only benefits pursuant to N.J.A.C. 10:71-2.2(e)2. He had not provided documentation indicating that he had not applied for retirement benefits or that he was not eligible for same. Also, he had not supplied sufficient documentation informing the Board how he covered his daily expenses. Thus, the Board was not effectively able to determine financial eligibility. R.E. v. Camdenn Cnty. Bd. of Social Serv., OAL Dkt. No. HMA 4310-14, 2014 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 373, Initial Decision (June 30, 2014). Denial of an application for Medicaid was affirmed when the applicant failed to provide verification of his address in the form requested pursuant to N.J.A.C. 10:70-2.3(a)1, N.J.A.C. 10:71-2.2(e)2, and N.J.A.C. 10:72-2.3(b). A letter from the landlord that was almost a year old was too old to verify the applicant's current address. A.M. v. Union Cnty. Bd. of Social Serv., OAL Dkt. No. HMA 07033-14, 2014 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 346, Initial Decision (July 16, 2014). When an applicant failed to provide sufficient verification pursuant to N.J.A.C. 10:71-2.2(e)2 for the Camden County Board of Social Services (CCBSS) to consider her application, she could not be considered eligible for Medicaid benefits. CCBSS notified the applicant's Power of Attorney (POA) several times of the verification documentation that was needed in order to establish eligibility, and the POA conceded that the requested

body: Page 13 of 14 § 10:71-2.2 Responsibilities in the application process documentation had not been provided. M.D. v. Camden Cnty. Bd. Social Serv., OAL Dkt. No. HMA 1459-14, 2014 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 281, Initial Decision (May 22, 2014). An Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) concluded that a county board of social services acted properly when it denied an application for Medicaid eligibility made by an applicant on a finding that the applicant had failed to provide the required verification. The applicant admitted that there were several outstanding requests for documents to which she had not responded. Because the board was required by N.J.A.C. 10:72-2.3(a) and N.J.A.C. 10:71-2.9 to verify all factors related to eligibility, including sources of income and resources, the applicant's conceded failure to comply with those requests per N.J.A.C. 10:71-2.2(e)1 and N.J.A.C. 10:71-3.1(b) to provide the requested items foreclosed a determination that she was eligible for Medicaid. M.D. v. Camden Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 1459-14, AGENCY DKT. NO. 410052818-01, 2014 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 273, Initial Decision (May 22, 2014). Applicant was not eligible for Medicaid benefits after failing to provide sufficient verification pursuant to N.J.A.C. 10:71-2.2(e)2. Although a request for certain bank statements was made on three separate occasions, the applicant produced no documents evidencing compliance with the request. Although he testified that the account might not have existed at the time in question, he produced no evidence of this fact. G.W. v. Camden Cnty. Bd. of Social Serv., OAL Dkt. No. HMA 15781-13, 2014 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 264, Initial Decision (May 12, 2014). Camden County Board of Social Services appropriately denied an application for Medicaid under N.J.A.C. 10:71- 2.2(e)2 when the applicant failed to establish by a preponderance of credible evidence that he provided all of the information necessary to complete his application for benefits. The Board twice notified the applicant of verification documentation that was needed in order for him to establish eligibility. Though he did provide some bank statements as well as handwritten notations on the Board's notice, the applicant did not submit all of the requested information. He admitted as much to a Board worker during a telephone conversation after he received the Board's denial notice. W.B. v. Div. of Medical Assistance and Health Serv. and Camden Cnty. Bd. of Social Serv., OAL Dkt. No. HMA 8393-13, 2014 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 252, Initial Decision (May 6, 2014). An Administrative Law Judge concluded that even though an elderly woman's application for Medicaid's Global Options Assisted Living Waiver Program was not processed in accordance with the requirements in N.J.A.C. 10:71- 2.2 and N.J.A.C. 10:71-2.3(c), the fact was that the applicant was not financially eligible for participation in the program. That is, the processing agencies' failure to comply with those requirements, including the 45-day processing requirement, did not provide a basis for an award of benefits to an otherwise ineligible applicant as such a retroactive award would be in contravention of N.J.A.C. 10:49-22.1(b). A.H. v. Div. of Med. Assistance & Health Servs. and Morris Cnty. Bd. of Soc. Servs., OAL Dkt. No. HMA 00531-13, 2014 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 91, Initial Decision (January 27, 2014). Initial Decision (2007 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 209) adopted, which concluded that an application for Medicaid benefits under the Medically Needy program was correctly denied for the applicant's failure to provide requested information regarding three attempts to sell the subject annuity, which the applicant claimed was an unavailable resource; while the Division may ultimately bear the burden of proving that a market exists, and that this particular annuity could be sold, this did not relieve the applicant of her obligation to produce information the Division requested. D.M. v. DMAHS, OAL Dkt. No. HMA 6394-06, 2007 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 546, Final Decision (June 11, 2007). Medicaid benefits properly provided despite non-compliance; status letter was lost in mail. B.W. v. Division of Medical Assistance and Health Services, 95 N.J.A.R.2d (DMA) 2. Patient not ineligible for Medicaid benefits when status letter containing necessary information from Medicaid office on eligibility was lost in mail. B.W. v. body: N.J.A.C. 10:71-2.3 This file includes all Regulations adopted and published through the New Jersey Register, Vol. 57 No. 12, June 16, 2025 NJ - New Jersey Administrative Code > TITLE 10. HUMAN SERVICES > CHAPTER 71. MEDICAID ONLY > SUBCHAPTER 2. THE APPLICATION PROCESS § 10:71-2.3 Policy and procedure on prompt disposition (a) The maximum period of time normally essential to process an application for the aged is 45 days; for the disabled or blind, 90 days. (b) "Date of effective disposition" based upon either administrative or board action means: 1. In the case of an approved application, the effective date of the application. (Either the date of application, or the date of form PA-1C, whichever is earlier); 2. In the case of a denied application, the date on which written notification informing the applicant of his or her lack of eligibility and the reason therefor is sent to him or her; 3. In the case of a withdrawn application, the date on which written notification confirming to the client that the agency has taken cognizance of his or her voluntary withdrawal is sent to him or her; or 4. In the case of a dismissed application, the date on which written notification informing the applicant of the dismissal and the reasons therefor is sent to him or her. (c) It is recognized that there will be exceptional cases where the proper processing of an application cannot be completed within the 45/90-day period. Where substantially reliable evidence of eligibility is still lacking at the end of the designated period, the application may be continued in pending status. In each such case, the CSSA shall be prepared to demonstrate that the delay resulted from one of the following: 1. Circumstances wholly within the applicant's control; 2. A determination to afford the applicant, whose proof of eligibility has been inconclusive, a further opportunity to develop additional evidence of eligibility before final action on his or her application; 3. An administrative or other emergency that could not reasonably have been avoided; or 4. Circumstances wholly outside the control of both the applicant and CSSA. (d) When the complete processing of an application is delayed beyond 45 days for the aged or 90 days for the blind or disabled, written notification shall be sent to the applicant on or before the expiration of such period, setting forth the specific reasons for delay. (e) Each county director of welfare shall arrange operational procedures and establish appropriate operational controls within his or her staff organization to expedite the processing of applications and assure the maximum possible compliance with these standards. (f) Control records on the exceptional cases shall disclose at any time the identity of all applications that have been in pending status beyond normal limits for processing and the reason therefor. Such record shall be adequate to make possible the preparation of a report of such information at any time it might be requested by the CSSA or the Division of Medical Assistance and Health Services. Annotations Notes Chapter Notes Case Notes Authorized representative of an applicant for Medicaid benefits failed to show that either the applicant's death, which occurred while the application was pending, or the death of her caseworker was the cause of the representative's failure to obtain and submit documentation requested in connection with the application. That was because much of the requested documentation that was still outstanding at the time of the denial of the application, from which this appeal was taken, was either requested while the applicant was still alive or was within the control of either the representative or the applicant's granddaughter. Thus, no exceptional circumstances existed justifying additional time to provide the requested documentation. E.W. v. DMAHS et al., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 03229-2021, 2021 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 421, Final Agency Determination (October 26, 2021). Where the applicant's Designated Authorized Representative (DAR) repeatedly failed to provide the requested documentation to determine eligibility, the Medicaid application was appropriately denied. The DAR and the applicant's spouse had 182 days from the first verification letter to the deadline set forth in the last verification letter to request, receive, and submit the information. The DAR's failure to timely request the documentation regarding the spouse's life insurance policy did not create a necessity for an extension of time. M.D. v. Div. of Med. Assistance and Health Servs., et al., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 11056-2020, 2021 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 234, Final Agency Determination (June 29, 2021). Social services board acted improperly when it refused to process a petitioner's Medicaid application on the ground that a certified translation of bank records that it had requested was not delivered by the September 5th deadline. Petitioner showed that she took reasonable steps to obtain the same and was able to obtain the translation by September 1. Because the next two days were legal holidays, petitioner should have been allotted the additional two days needed to mail the translation to the board. H.C. v. Hudson Cnty. Bd. of Soc. Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 14152-18, 2019 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 111, Final Agency Determination (January 22, 2019).

body: Page 3 of 12 § 10:71-2.3 Policy and procedure on prompt disposition Medicaid application was properly denied over the applicant's claim that the deadline should have been extended to allow him to provide requested items because the agency in fact had extended the deadline for receipt of the requested items from July 19 to December 13, and the applicant still failed to provide the needed documentation. M.S. v. Gloucester Cnty., Bd. of Soc. Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 02481-18, 2018 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 794, Final Agency Determination (June 25, 2018). Lawyers who were conservators for an elderly man who was applying for Medicaid nursing home disabled benefits were acting in good faith to transmit all required documentation to a county social services board and their conduct also reflected cooperation and proactive efforts to comply with the board's requests. Those efforts constituted "exceptional circumstances" within the meaning of Medicaid Communication 10-09 and justified an order reversing the benefit denial and requiring a review of the application. H.P. v. Ocean Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 01118-18, 2018 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 271, Initial Decision (May 11, 2018). DMAHS Director reversed an ALJ's Initial Decision in favor of a Medicaid applicant and reinstated an agency ruling denying benefits on the ground that the applicant failed to provide the needed information prior to the date on which benefits were denied and that the determination notice issued by the agency sufficiently set out the action that the agency was taking, the rationale therefor and the statutes that supported the proposed action. D.C. v. DMAHS, OAL DKT. NO. HMA 06870-17, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 1310, Final Agency Determination (December 7, 2017). Determination of county social services board denying a Medicaid application made on behalf of a disabled woman who died during the pendency of the proceedings was rejected by an ALJ on findings that the board failed to comply with the 90-day statutory time frame for decision, failed to advise the applicant's representative as to why the application was not being determined on a timely basis, allowed 570 days to elapse between the date of application and the date of denial, and otherwise failed to comply with its obligations vis-a-vis the application. D.C. v. Burlington Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 6870-17, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 727, Initial Decision (September 18, 2017). Failure on the part of an applicant for Medicaid Nursing Home Benefits to timely provide requested financial documentation needed to establish eligibility provided grounds for a determination denying benefits to the applicant. The regulation's use of the word "may" demonstrated that the agency had the discretion to either put the application into pending status or not, and the exhibition of a purported "spirit of cooperation" on the part of the applicant did not obviate the agency's ability to issue a denial letter where, as here, the applicant continued to fail to provide financial information as requested. E.Z. v. Bergen Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 07334-17, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 728, Initial Decision (September 15, 2017). Medicaid application for a husband who was separated from his wife was properly denied because the husband failed to document any efforts that he ostensibly had made to obtain financial data possessed by his wife. Even though the husband insisted that he could not obtain any information from her, the husband lived next door to the wife, the husband was responsible for the couple's children, the wife had signed a contract obligating her to provide medical care to the husband and the couple had a joint checking account, jointly owned real estate and had filed a joint Chapter 7 case. R.W. v. Somerset Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 17759-16, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 691, Initial Decision (September 13, 2017). The agency's failure to comply with the regulatory deadlines for the processing of a Medicaid application notwithstanding, the applicant did not comply with proper requests for documentation concerning a special needs trust and certain insurance and annuity policies with the result that the agency could not verify the applicant's resources and properly denied the application on that basis. K.S. v. DMAHS, OAL DKT. NO. HMA 14539-16, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 705, Initial Decision (September 7, 2017). County social services board did not comply with its obligations to process a Medicaid application within 45 days nor did it provide a reason for delaying its processing of the applicant's application, thereby violating governing law. However, its determination granting retroactive coverage only for two of three months was proper because the

body: Page 4 of 12 § 10:71-2.3 Policy and procedure on prompt disposition applicant was ineligible by reason of resources during the third month. B.B. v. Ocean Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 628-17, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 649, Initial Decision (August 24, 2017). Failure by a social services board to process an application for Medicaid benefits within the 45-day period imposed by law was not excused by the fact that the caseworker assigned to the file died during that period because there was no reason why the file should not have been timely reassigned to another caseworker. J.D. v. Essex Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 03198-17, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 398, Initial Decision (June 20, 2017). Director approved of and adopted ALJ's report and recommendation finding that the failure and/or refusal of a husband of an incapacitated wife to disclose his resources in connection with a redetermination of the wife's Medicaid eligibility did not provide grounds to either extend the time for compliance or grant a "spousal waiver." K.Z. v. DMAHS, OAL DKT. NO. HMA 16945-16, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 1143, Final Agency Determination (May 23, 2017). Agency's denial of an application for Medicaid nursing home benefits on the ground that agency requests for information were unfulfilled was reversed because, unbeknown to the agency, applicant's wife, who was responding to the agency's information requests, had been hospitalized as a result of a fall and spent several weeks in a rehabilitation facility. Given those unforeseen circumstances, the applicant's wife should have been allowed additional time to respond to the agency's follow-up requests. R.B. v. Burlington Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NOS. HMA 14375-16, HMA 04295-16 (Consolidated), 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 313, Initial Decision (May 15, 2017). ALJ's determination that an applicant's first Medicaid application was properly denied was approved by the Director, but the ALJ's finding reversing the county social services board's ruling that a second application should not be denied was rejected by the Director. The fact that the applicant's wife, who was responding to the agency's information requests, had been hospitalized due to a fall and had spent several weeks in a rehabilitation facility was an insufficient basis for relief because the applicant at all times was represented by counsel. That meant that "exceptional circumstances" justifying an extension of the deadline for submission of verifications were not shown. R.B. v. DMAHS, OAL DKT. NO. HMA 04295-16, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 1169, Final Agency Determination (May 13, 2017). Failure and/or refusal of the husband of an incapacitated wife who was receiving long-term nursing home services to provide disclosure of his resources as needed for a redetermination of the wife's eligibility did not provide grounds for an order either extending the time for compliance or granting a "spousal waiver." Counsel to the nursing home, which had initiated the redetermination process in January 2016 on behalf of the wife, did not take any steps to include the recalcitrant husband in a motion for an order to show cause compelling the wife's son, who was her guardian, to cooperate in the redetermination process. Nor was a "spousal waiver" appropriate on these facts. K.Z. v. Bergen Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 16945-16, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 219, Initial Decision (April 5, 2017). Applicant for Medicaid won limited relief on claims that her eligibility date was properly based on an application that she made on May 8, 2015 as opposed to on a second application dated August 23, 2016. The social services board had violated various regulations in connection with the earlier application, which it apparently had misplaced, so it was properly ordered to dispose of the May 8 application within 45 days of the ruling. S.D. v. Essex Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 02582-17, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 181, Initial Decision (March 29, 2017). ALJ rejected a determination that an applicant was ineligible for Medicaid on findings that in fact she had substantively demonstrated financial eligibility. The application languished for almost 250 days, well beyond the timelines imposed by governing law, and then was denied on a finding that the applicant's resources were $ 0.21 over the maximum. Since that amount would plainly be rounded down under most accounting protocols, the denial was arbitrary and capricious. M.R. v. Morris Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 17658-16, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 147, Initial Decision (March 9, 2017).

body: Page 5 of 12 § 10:71-2.3 Policy and procedure on prompt disposition Agency's denial of a Medicaid application based on the applicant's failure to provide requested information was reversed because the applicant had made many attempts to obtain them. The agency, though required to assist the applicant, in fact had made no effort to assist by utilizing either AVS or PARIS and thus could not properly deny the application based on missing information. Moreover, the resulting delay was beyond the applicant's control and could not be used as a basis for denial. C.F.J. v. Hudson Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 06589-16 (Remand of HMA 04859-14), 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 50, Initial Decision (January 31, 2017). Original denial of Medicaid application was proper despite the fact that the applicant belatedly provided requested documentation because the applicant's failure to timely provide such verifications that led to the denial. It was not the agency's duty to organize and summarize raw data in the form of deposit slips or checking-account registers to determine dates of deposits and expenses paid by the applicant and/or family members in order to determine eligibility. V.W. v. DMAHS, OAL DKT. NO. HMA 12941-16, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 52, Initial Decision (January 27, 2017). Medicaid applicant won retroactive eligibility date because the social services agency responsible for acting on his application failed to timely move the case through the approval process, failed to give the applicant required notifications, failed to assist the applicant and failed to independently verify the value of resources. The overall failure on the part of the agency justified a retroactive date. W.M. v. Union Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 11651-16, 2017 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 27, Initial Decision (January 18, 2017). Agency rejected a Medicaid applicant's exceptions to denial of benefits that was based on the failure by applicant and/or her designated, authorized representative to provide information on certain insurance policies. Although that information in fact was provided more than a month after the deadline, there was nothing in the record to demonstrate they either asked for or that there were exceptional circumstances warranting additional time to provide the requested verifications. J.B. v. DMAHS, OAL DKT. NO. HMA 9587-2016, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 1374, Final Administrative Determination (December 15, 2016). Failure on the part of the representative for a nursing home resident to submit required documentation despite the issuance of numerous extensions of the deadline afforded grounds for a denial of Medicaid eligibility. A.D. v. Cape May Cnty. Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 10418-16, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 1236, Initial Decision (December 8, 2016). County social services board did not comply with its obligations to process a Medicaid application made by an institutionalized man within 45 days nor did it comply with its obligation to provide a reason for the delay. That said, the board's conduct did not justify an exception from the rule that the date of funding of a Qualified Income Trust (QIT) was determinative of the month of Medicaid eligibility, and the determination on that issue was properly approved. J.E. v. Passaic Cnty., Bd. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 10553-2016, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 1010, Initial Decision (December 5, 2016). Though the ALJ recognized that employee of a county social services board had mishandled the Medicaid application made by a husband on behalf of his institutionalized wife, the ALJ lacked the power to provide an "equitable" remedy because the wife was not Medicaid-eligible until the spend-down was completed. However, the ALJ encouraged the Commissioner to exercise any discretion possessed by the Commissioner's office in order to address the seemingly unfair result. A.S. v. DMAHS and Monmouth Cnty. Div. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 13504-16, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 1015, Initial Decision (November 4, 2016). Though the agency failed to promptly process an application for Medicaid Only nursing home benefits and failed to advise the applicant of the reason for delay, the failure of the agency to advise the applicant of what needed to occur for eligibility to be determined was not grounds for an eligibility date that was earlier than that granted by the agency because the applicant was not resource-eligible earlier than the date awarded. W.H. v. Monmouth Cnty. Div. of Social Servs., OAL DKT. NO. HMA 10917-16, 2016 N.J. AGEN LEXIS 862, Initial Decision (October 19, 2016).
